lessons.title: Ownership
lessons.content:
# Ownership

Ownership is Rust's most unique feature and enables memory safety without a garbage collector.

### Three Rules of Ownership
1. Each value in Rust has a variable that's called its owner.
2. There can only be one owner at a time.
3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value will be dropped.

```rust
let s1 = String::from("hello");
let s2 = s1; // s1 is moved to s2 and is no longer valid
```

lessons.title: References & Borrowing
lessons.content:
# References & Borrowing

Borrowing allows you to use a value without taking ownership of it.

### Rules of Borrowing
1. At any given time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references.
2. References must always be valid.

```rust
fn calculate_length(s: &String) -> usize { // s is a reference
    s.len()
}
```

Structs & Enums
lessons.content:
# Structs & Enums

### Structs
Used to create custom data types.
```rust
struct User {
    username: String,
    active: bool,
}
```

### Enums
Allow you to enumerate over possible variants. Rust enums are very powerful as they can hold data.
```rust
enum Message {
    Quit,
    Move { x: i32, y: i32 },
    Write(String),
}
```

lessons.title: Pattern Matching
lessons.content:
# Pattern Matching

The `match` control flow operator allows you to compare a value against a series of patterns.

```rust
let some_u8_value = 0u8;
match some_u8_value {
    1 => println!("one"),
    3 => println!("three"),
    _ => (), // placeholder for all other values
}
```
It is exhaustive, meaning you must handle every possible case.
